rounds.proof_sketch: Block size is fixed at 256, so threadIdx.x ∈ [0,255]. shared_mem is accessed only via shared_mem[tid] and shared_mem[tid+stride]. Maximum access index = max(tid+stride) = 127+128 = 255. The element at index 256 in the mutated array is never read or written.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes the shared memory allocation from 256 to 257 floats, but the kernel's execution only accesses indices 0-255. The thread index tid = threadIdx.x is bounded by blockDim.x = 256, so tid ∈ [0,255]. In the parallel reduction loop, the maximum index accessed is tid + stride where the largest case is tid=127 with stride=128, giving index 255. The extra element at index 256 is allocated but never touched by any thread in any block. Since no code path reads from or writes to shared_mem[256], the computation is identical to the original kernel for all possible input values.
rounds.kill_strategy: This mutant is unkillable because the mutation only allocates one extra unused shared memory element. The kernel's access patterns are determined entirely by the fixed block_size=256, which bounds all thread indices to [0,255]. No input values can cause the kernel to access shared_mem[256].
rounds.recommendations: Mutation testing tools should recognize that changes to array allocation sizes that exceed the maximum accessed index are semantically equivalent when index bounds are statically determinable. A static analysis pass could identify that shared_mem's actual usage is bounded by blockDim.x-1=255, making any allocation ≥256 equivalent.
